Mortimer finally reveals that he found fresh footprints near the body which he identifies as those of a gigantic hound.

s: The investigation into Sir Charles's death has not yet formally begun, but Holmes identifies two initial questions: whether a crime was committed and what the crime was and how it occurred. He begins by analyzing the footprints, Sir Charles's movements, the moor-gate, and the possibility that someone or something frightened him into running.

l: The Hound of the Baskervilles, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 4.
s: Sherlock Holmes interviews Sir Henry Baskerville, who has received a warning letter telling him to keep away from the moor and has lost one of his newly purchased boots. Holmes determines that the warning message was assembled from words cut out of a Times leading article, with “moor” written in ink, and infers that its educated sender tried to disguise his writing. Dr. Mortimer then explains Sir Henry’s inheritance, his uncle’s death, and the family story of the hound. Despite the possible danger, Sir Henry insists that he will go to Baskerville Hall and invites Holmes and Dr. Watson to lunch at the Northumberland Hotel.

l: Sherlock Holmes, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 4.
s: Sherlock Holmes examines Sir Henry Baskerville’s warning letter and identifies its words as having been cut from a Times leading article. He infers that the sender was educated, attempted to disguise his handwriting, used nail-scissors and gum, and probably composed the message in a hotel near Charing Cross. He discusses the possible danger of Sir Henry going to Baskerville Hall and agrees to meet him and Dr. Watson for lunch.

l: Dr. Watson, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 4.
s: Dr. Watson is present during Holmes’s interview with Dr. Mortimer and Sir Henry Baskerville. He supplies Holmes with the Times and initially fails to see the connection between the newspaper article and the warning message. He agrees to lunch with Sir Henry and Holmes at the Northumberland Hotel.

l: Dr. Mortimer, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 4.
s: Dr. Mortimer brings Sir Henry Baskerville to meet Sherlock Holmes and helps present the case concerning the Baskerville family. He argues that the warning letter may have come from someone convinced that the business was supernatural. He believes Sir Henry’s missing boot was merely mislaid and later tells Sir Henry the full account of his inheritance and his uncle’s death.

l: Sir Henry Baskerville, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 4.
s: Sir Henry Baskerville meets Sherlock Holmes after receiving a warning telling him to keep away from the moor. He reports that one of a pair of new tan boots disappeared from outside his hotel room, and he insists that he will go to the home of his own people despite the possible danger. He asks for time to consider the information and invites Holmes and Dr. Watson to lunch.

l: the Baskerville family, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 4.
s: The Baskerville family is associated with a long-standing story about a hound, which Sir Henry has heard since childhood. Sir Henry is the last representative of the family and has inherited its estate after his uncle’s death.

l: London, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 4.
s: Sir Henry has spent nearly all his time in the United States and Canada and is new to British life. He arrives in London, shops for clothing and boots, receives the warning letter, and plans to return to the Northumberland Hotel.

l: Northumberland Hotel, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 4.
s: Sir Henry is staying at the Northumberland Hotel when the warning letter addressed to him arrives. Holmes infers from the pen and ink that the address may have been written in a hotel and suggests that the sender might be found by examining hotel waste-paper baskets around Charing Cross.

l: Baskerville Hall, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 4.
s: Baskerville Hall is the home of Sir Henry’s people and the destination under consideration after his inheritance. Although Holmes warns that there may be danger there, Sir Henry declares that no person or devil will prevent him from going.

l: Dartmoor, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 4.
s: The moor is the place from which the warning message tells Sir Henry to keep away. Holmes and Dr. Mortimer consider the warning evidence that someone knows more than they do about what happens there.

l: the warning letter, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 4.
s: The warning letter is a greyish envelope addressed in rough printed characters to Sir Henry Baskerville at the Northumberland Hotel. It contains a folded half-sheet of foolscap with a message assembled from pasted printed words, and it was posted from Charing Cross the previous evening.

l: the warning letter to Sir Henry, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 4.
s: The warning message says, “As you value your life or your reason keep away from the moor.” All its words except “moor” are pasted onto the paper from printed material, and Holmes concludes that the sender took pains to hide identifying clues.

l: the Hound of the Baskervilles, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 4.
s: The hound is part of the Baskerville family’s traditional story and has been told as a pet story since Sir Henry was in the nursery. Sir Henry has not previously taken the story seriously, although it is considered in connection with his uncle’s death and the family’s affairs.

l: the inheritance, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 4.
s: Sir Henry has inherited the Baskerville family estate after his uncle’s death. He says that he has come into the inheritance “with a vengeance” and must decide whether to proceed to Baskerville Hall.

l: the Baskerville curse, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 4.
s: The unit discusses the family’s story of the hound and whether the events surrounding the inheritance and the uncle’s death are supernatural. Sir Henry refers to the possibility of a family fiend, while Holmes and Dr. Mortimer also consider danger from human beings.

l: the danger on the moor, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 4.
s: Holmes believes there may be danger connected with Sir Henry’s going to Baskerville Hall. The warning may have been intended to protect Sir Henry, or it may have been sent to frighten him away for someone else’s purposes.

l: the planned journey to Baskerville Hall, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 4.
s: The planned journey to Baskerville Hall is the main practical decision facing Sir Henry. Despite warnings of possible supernatural or human danger, he firmly decides that he will go and asks for time to think before giving Holmes and Dr. Watson his final view.

l: the newspaper clipping message, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 4.
s: The newspaper clipping message was formed by cutting words from the Times’s leading article on free trade and pasting them onto a blank half-sheet of foolscap. Holmes identifies the source from the distinctive type, observes that “keep away” and “from the” were cut as single pieces, and concludes that “moor” was written in ink because it could not be found in print.

l: The Hound of the Baskervilles, The Hound of the Baskervilles, We heard the steps of our visitors descend the stair and the bang
s: Holmes and Watson follow Dr. Mortimer and Baskerville from their lodgings in an attempt to identify the person shadowing Baskerville. The unknown pursuer, traveling in hansom cab No. 2704 and disguised with a bushy black beard, notices them and escapes down Regent Street. Holmes admits that his eagerness caused them to lose the man, though he had obtained the cab number. He then sends Cartwright to investigate the waste-paper of twenty-three nearby hotels for a cut-out center page of The Times and plans to identify the cabman by wire.

l: Sherlock Holmes, The Hound of the Baskervilles, We heard the steps of our visitors descend the stair and the bang
s: Holmes changes quickly from a languid dreamer into a man of action and follows Dr. Mortimer and Baskerville with Watson. He recognizes that a cab is following them, but his eagerness to pursue it betrays him and allows the unknown man to escape. Holmes records the cab number as 2704, sends Cartwright to search hotel waste-paper, and plans to identify the cabman by wire.

l: Dr. Watson, The Hound of the Baskervilles, We heard the steps of our visitors descend the stair and the bang
s: Watson follows Holmes in pursuit of Dr. Mortimer and Baskerville. He sees the pursuer's bushy black beard and piercing eyes but cannot swear to the man's face. Holmes asks Watson to record this failure alongside his successes.

l: Dr. Mortimer, The Hound of the Baskervilles, We heard the steps of our visitors descend the stair and the bang
s: Dr. Mortimer leaves with Baskerville and walks ahead of Holmes and Watson toward Oxford Street and Regent Street. He and Baskerville eventually vanish from Holmes and Watson's view.

l: Sir Henry Baskerville, The Hound of the Baskervilles, We heard the steps of our visitors descend the stair and the bang
s: Baskerville leaves with Dr. Mortimer and is followed through the streets by an unknown person. Holmes concludes that Baskerville has been closely shadowed since arriving in town, including after choosing the Northumberland Hotel.

l: unknown pursuer (Baskerville's shadow), The Hound of the Baskervilles, We heard the steps of our visitors descend the stair and the bang
s: The unknown pursuer follows Baskerville in a hansom cab, apparently so that he can loiter behind or move ahead without being noticed. He has a bushy black beard that Holmes suspects was false and escapes after detecting Holmes and Watson.

l: Cartwright, The Hound of the Baskervilles, We heard the steps of our visitors descend the stair and the bang
s: Cartwright, a fourteen-year-old district messenger with a bright, keen face, is assigned by Holmes to visit twenty-three nearby hotels. He is to search their waste-paper for a center page of The Times with holes cut in it and report by wire before evening.

l: Northumberland Hotel, The Hound of the Baskervilles, We heard the steps of our visitors descend the stair and the bang
s: The Northumberland Hotel is the hotel Baskerville chose. Holmes reasons that the pursuer learned of this choice quickly, suggesting that Baskerville was being closely followed.

l: hansom cab No. 2704, The Hound of the Baskervilles, We heard the steps of our visitors descend the stair and the bang
s: Hansom cab No. 2704 carries the unknown pursuer as he follows Baskerville. The pursuer escapes in it after seeing Holmes and Watson, and Holmes intends to discover the identity of its cabman by wire.

l: the twenty-three nearby hotels, The Hound of the Baskervilles, We heard the steps of our visitors descend the stair and the bang
s: The twenty-three nearby hotels are listed in the Hotel Directory and are all in the immediate neighborhood of Charing Cross. Cartwright is instructed to visit each one and ask to inspect its waste-paper from the previous day.

l: The Times, The Hound of the Baskervilles, We heard the steps of our visitors descend the stair and the bang
s: Holmes gives Cartwright a copy of The Times and identifies the page he must search for in hotel waste-paper. The page is the center page, marked by holes cut with scissors.

l: cut-out center page of The Times, The Hound of the Baskervilles, We heard the steps of our visitors descend the stair and the bang
s: The cut-out center page of The Times is the object Holmes wants Cartwright to find. Cartwright is told to recognize it by comparing it with the copy Holmes provides.

l: waste-paper from the hotels, The Hound of the Baskervilles, We heard the steps of our visitors descend the stair and the bang
s: The waste-paper from the hotels may contain the cut-out center page of The Times. Holmes expects that in most hotels it will already have been burned or removed, while only three may still have heaps of paper available for searching.

l: Baskerville's shadowing, The Hound of the Baskervilles, We heard the steps of our visitors descend the stair and the bang
s: Baskerville's shadowing is revealed by the pursuer's rapid knowledge of Baskerville's hotel and continued following through London. Holmes believes the pursuer used a cab to remain hidden, follow or pass Baskerville, and be ready to follow if Baskerville hired a cab.

l: Holmes and Watson's pursuit, The Hound of the Baskervilles, We heard the steps of our visitors descend the stair and the bang
s: Holmes and Watson follow Dr. Mortimer and Baskerville while trying to identify Baskerville's invisible attendant. They approach the pursuer's cab, but the pursuer recognizes them and escapes before they can obtain more than the cab number.

l: Cartwright's hotel investigation, The Hound of the Baskervilles, We heard the steps of our visitors descend the stair and the bang
s: Cartwright's hotel investigation requires visits to twenty-three hotels, payments to the outside and hall porters, and a search for the cut-out center page of The Times. Holmes gives him additional money for emergencies and requests a wire report at Baker Street before evening.

l: The Hound of the Baskervilles, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 5.
s: Sherlock Holmes investigates the surveillance and strange incidents surrounding Sir Henry Baskerville, including the theft and return of Sir Henry's boots and the black-bearded spy who followed him. Holmes learns that the suspected watchers are staying at other hotels rather than the Northumberland Hotel, while a telegram confirms that Barrymore is at Baskerville Hall. Sir Henry decides to go to Devonshire, and Dr. Watson agrees to accompany him because Holmes cannot leave London indefinitely. The cabman John Clayton reveals that the spy falsely identified himself as Sherlock Holmes, causing Holmes to lose his third investigative lead and worry about Watson's safety.

l: Sherlock Holmes, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 5.
s: Sherlock Holmes examines the Northumberland Hotel register, investigates the surveillance of Sir Henry Baskerville, and questions the financial circumstances surrounding Sir Charles Baskerville's will and estate. He arranges telegrams to verify Barrymore's whereabouts, recruits Dr. Watson to accompany Sir Henry, and questions John Clayton about the black-bearded spy. Holmes concludes that three investigative leads have failed in London and becomes concerned about sending Watson to Devonshire.

l: Dr. Watson, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 5.
s: Dr. Watson accompanies Sherlock Holmes and Sir Henry Baskerville during the investigation. He agrees to go with Sir Henry to Baskerville Hall and report carefully to Holmes, despite Holmes's warning that the business is dangerous.

l: Sir Henry Baskerville, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 5.
s: Sir Henry Baskerville is angered by the disappearance of one brown boot and one black boot, though the brown boot later reappears under a cabinet. He plans to go to Baskerville Hall at the end of the week and asks Dr. Watson to accompany him. He has not yet made a will and says that the money should remain with the title and estate.

l: Dr. Mortimer, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 5.
s: Dr. Mortimer tells Holmes that Barrymore is a full-bearded man in charge of Baskerville Hall and that Barrymore and his wife each received five hundred pounds from Sir Charles Baskerville. He says that he received a thousand pounds and explains the succession of the Baskerville estate if Sir Henry dies.

l: Sir Charles Baskerville, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 5.
s: Sir Charles Baskerville left five hundred pounds each to Barrymore and his wife, a thousand pounds to Dr. Mortimer, other smaller sums and charitable bequests, and the residue to Sir Henry Baskerville. His estate was worth close to a million, and his will becomes an important subject in assessing possible motives.

l: Barrymore, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 5.
s: Barrymore is the son of the former caretaker and has served the Baskervilles for generations with his wife. Holmes suspects that his appearance could match the black-bearded spy, but a telegram confirms that Barrymore is at Baskerville Hall.

l: the Baskerville family, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 5.
s: The Baskerville family is represented in the succession by Sir Henry Baskerville and, if he dies, by the distant Desmond cousins. The family title, house, land, and money are discussed as assets that Sir Henry believes should remain together.

l: Northumberland Hotel, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 5.
s: The Northumberland Hotel is where Sir Henry Baskerville is staying and where Holmes examines the register. Holmes learns that the people interested in Sir Henry are staying elsewhere, apparently watching him without wanting to be seen.

l: Baskerville Hall, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 5.
s: Baskerville Hall is the Devonshire residence to which Sir Henry Baskerville plans to return. Barrymore is reported to be present there and in charge of the Hall.

l: Baker Street, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 5.
s: Baker Street is Sherlock Holmes's residence and the place to which Holmes and Dr. Watson return after meeting Sir Henry. John Clayton comes there to answer Holmes's questions about the cab passenger who followed them.

l: London, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 5.
s: London is the setting for the surveillance of Sir Henry Baskerville and the investigation into the connected mysteries. Holmes decides that the city's size makes it difficult to identify the watchers, and he remains there because of his consulting practice and another important case.

l: Devonshire, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 5.
s: Devonshire is the destination for Sir Henry Baskerville and Dr. Watson when they leave London. Holmes believes that the investigation may have better prospects there, although he warns Watson that the situation is dangerous.

l: Dartmoor, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 5.
s: Dartmoor is the region where Baskerville Hall is located and where Sir Henry Baskerville is expected to go. Holmes says he cannot be absent from London for an indefinite time to travel there.

l: Sir Henry's missing boots, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 5.
s: One of Sir Henry Baskerville's new brown boots disappears, followed by one of his old black boots. The brown boot is later found under a cabinet, although no one explains how it got there, adding another unexplained incident to the investigation.

l: Stapleton, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 5.
s: The black-bearded spy watches Sherlock Holmes's house and follows Sir Henry Baskerville and Dr. Watson in a cab. He hires John Clayton, falsely claims to be a detective named Sherlock Holmes, and escapes through Waterloo Station after anticipating that Holmes would trace the cab.

l: Sir Charles Baskerville's will, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 5.
s: Sir Charles Baskerville's will provides five hundred pounds each to Barrymore and his wife, a thousand pounds to Dr. Mortimer, smaller sums to others, and the residue to Sir Henry Baskerville. It also raises questions about who would inherit if Sir Henry died and about whether the beneficiaries might have motives.

l: the Baskerville estate, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 5.
s: The Baskerville estate is worth close to a million, including a residue of seven hundred and forty thousand pounds after the other provisions described by Dr. Mortimer. The estate is entailed to the Desmonds if Sir Henry dies, while Sir Henry wants the money to remain with the title and property.

l: Sir Charles Baskerville's death, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 5.
s: Sir Charles Baskerville's death remains the central background to the investigation. Holmes considers the death together with the surveillance, the boot incidents, and the other recent mysteries as part of an unusually complex case.

l: the surveillance of Sir Henry Baskerville, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 5.
s: The surveillance of Sir Henry Baskerville continues in London through watchers who stay at hotels other than the Northumberland Hotel. A black-bearded man follows Sir Henry and Dr. Watson, but his identity and purpose remain unknown after he deceives Holmes through the cabman.

l: the investigation, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 5.
s: The investigation follows several leads: the hotel register, the missing boots, Barrymore's location, the financial interests in Sir Charles Baskerville's will, and the cabman who drove the spy. Holmes loses the leads concerning the hotel watchers, the newspaper clipping, and the cabman, leaving him to hope that the investigation will progress when Watson reaches Devonshire.

l: The Hound of the Baskervilles, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 6.
s: Sir Henry Baskerville, Dr. Watson, and Dr. Mortimer travel from London to Devonshire and arrive at Baskerville Hall, where Barrymore and his wife receive them. Sherlock Holmes instructs Dr. Watson to report facts, keep Sir Henry under close protection, and investigate the people surrounding him on the moor. During the journey, they learn that Selden, the Notting Hill murderer, has escaped from Princetown and is hiding somewhere nearby. That night, Dr. Watson hears a woman sobbing somewhere inside Baskerville Hall.

l: Baskerville Hall, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 6.
s: Baskerville Hall is the ancient home of the Baskerville family, with ivy-covered granite walls, twin towers, a dark avenue, and a large, heavily timbered hall. Sir Henry Baskerville and Dr. Watson arrive there, and Barrymore and his wife receive them. During the night, Dr. Watson hears the sound of a woman crying somewhere in the house.

l: Sir Henry Baskerville, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 6.
s: Sir Henry Baskerville travels with Dr. Watson and Dr. Mortimer to Devonshire to take possession of Baskerville Hall. He is delighted by the Devon scenery and eager to see the moor, but the atmosphere of Baskerville Hall makes him uneasy. He plans to install powerful electric lamps along the dark avenue.

l: Dr. Watson, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 6.
s: Dr. Watson travels to Devonshire with Sir Henry Baskerville and Dr. Mortimer at Sherlock Holmes’s direction. Holmes tells him to report all facts, especially information about Sir Henry’s neighbours and the death of Sir Charles Baskerville, and to keep his revolver close. At Baskerville Hall, Dr. Watson hears a woman sobbing during the night.

l: Sherlock Holmes, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 6.
s: Sherlock Holmes accompanies Dr. Watson to the station and instructs him to report facts rather than theories. He says that James Desmond can probably be eliminated from consideration, but that the Barrymore couple and the other people around Sir Henry must remain under suspicion. Holmes also warns Sir Henry not to go about alone, to keep his revolver near him, and to avoid the moor at night.

l: Dr. Mortimer, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 6.
s: Dr. Mortimer travels with Sir Henry Baskerville and Dr. Watson to Devonshire. He says that he and Sir Henry have not been shadowed during the previous two days, although they separated for parts of the previous day. He leaves Baskerville Hall after bringing Sir Henry and Dr. Watson there because his wife is expecting him.

l: Sir Charles Baskerville, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 6.
s: Sir Charles Baskerville formerly lived a very retired life at Baskerville Hall. Barrymore and his wife were strongly attached to him, and his death shocked them and made the house painful for them. The new building at the estate was begun with money from Sir Charles’s South African gold.

l: Barrymore couple, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 6.
s: The Barrymore couple have served the Baskerville family for several generations and looked after Sir Charles Baskerville. They remain on Sherlock Holmes’s list of suspects because Holmes does not want to dismiss them without determining whether they are innocent or guilty. They tell Sir Henry that they may eventually leave Baskerville Hall because of their painful memories of Sir Charles’s death.

l: Barrymore, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 6.
s: Barrymore receives Sir Henry Baskerville and Dr. Watson at Baskerville Hall, helps with their luggage, and offers to serve dinner. He explains that he and his wife may leave when it is convenient because they were attached to Sir Charles Baskerville and find the house painful after his death. He shows Sir Henry and Dr. Watson to their rooms and the dining room.

l: Selden, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 6.
s: Selden is identified as the Notting Hill murderer, whose conduct was marked by peculiar ferocity and wanton brutality. He has escaped from Princetown and has been at large for three days while warders watch the roads and stations. The driver says that Selden would stop at nothing and may be hiding somewhere on the moor.

l: Devonshire, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 6.
s: Sir Henry Baskerville, Dr. Watson, and Dr. Mortimer travel to Devonshire by train. The countryside is described as greener, damper, and more rugged than the country they have left, with granite, wooded valleys, and moorland rising in the distance. Sir Henry recognizes its familiar features and expresses strong affection for the county.

l: Dartmoor, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 6.
s: The moor first appears to the travelers as a grey, melancholy hill with a jagged summit. As they approach Baskerville Hall, it becomes a vast, bleak, desolate landscape of tors, cairns, boulders, and cold wind. Sherlock Holmes warns Sir Henry to avoid it during the hours of darkness.

l: the Baskerville family, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 6.
s: The Baskerville family has lived at Baskerville Hall for five hundred years and has left a deep mark on the area. Sir Henry Baskerville is described as a proud, strong, and fiery descendant of that line. The family’s ancestors are depicted in portraits and coats of arms throughout the hall.

l: the Baskerville legend, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 6.
s: The Baskerville legend is described as a queer old legend that Dr. Mortimer has read to Sherlock Holmes and the others. Holmes reminds Sir Henry of its warning to avoid the moor during the dark hours when the powers of evil are exalted.

l: the persecution of Sir Henry Baskerville, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 6.
s: Sherlock Holmes considers whether James Desmond, the next heir, could be responsible for the persecution of Sir Henry Baskerville. He concludes that Desmond’s amiable disposition makes this unlikely and says that Desmond can be eliminated from consideration.

l: Sir Charles Baskerville's death, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 6.
s: Sherlock Holmes asks Dr. Watson to seek fresh particulars concerning the death of Sir Charles Baskerville. Barrymore and his wife say that Sir Charles’s death shocked them and made their surroundings at Baskerville Hall painful.

l: Selden's prison escape, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 6.
s: Selden has escaped from Princetown and has been at large for three days. Warders watch the roads and stations, while local farmers fear encountering him despite the five-pound reward for information.

l: the train journey to Devonshire, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 6.
s: The train journey to Devonshire is swift and pleasant. Dr. Watson becomes better acquainted with Sir Henry Baskerville and Dr. Mortimer, while Sir Henry watches the changing countryside and eagerly recognizes the Devon scenery. During the journey, Dr. Mortimer points out the first sight of the moor.

l: the Baskerville estate, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 6.
s: The Baskerville estate includes the lodge-gates, a long tree-lined avenue, the moorland surroundings, and Baskerville Hall itself. The lodge is partly ruined, while a new building begun with Sir Charles Baskerville’s South African gold stands nearby. The estate appears beautiful to Sir Henry but dark and melancholy to Dr. Watson.

l: the woman crying in Baskerville Hall, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 6.
s: The woman crying in Baskerville Hall is heard by Dr. Watson in the middle of the night. He identifies the sound as a woman’s sob, a muffled and strangling gasp caused by uncontrollable sorrow. He believes the sound is inside the house and not far away, but hears nothing further for half an hour.

l: The Hound of the Baskervilles, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 7.
s: Dr. Watson investigates the Barrymores’ account of the telegram and suspects that Barrymore may have been in London when Sir Charles Baskerville died. On the moor, Watson meets Jack Stapleton, a naturalist from Merripit House, who discusses Sir Charles’s death, the Baskerville family legend, and the dangers of the Grimpen Mire. Stapleton brings Watson toward Merripit House, where Watson encounters Beryl Stapleton, who secretly warns him to return to London and leave the moor. During their walk, Watson and Stapleton hear a strange cry that Stapleton attributes possibly to a bittern, though local peasants call it the Baskerville hound.

l: Dr. Watson, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 7.
s: Dr. Watson questions the Grimpen postmaster and his son about whether Barrymore personally received Holmes’s test telegram, but learns only that it was given to Mrs. Barrymore. He then meets Jack Stapleton, walks across the moor with him, hears the Hound’s cry, and is secretly warned by Beryl Stapleton to return to London.

l: Sir Henry Baskerville, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 7.
s: Sir Henry Baskerville agrees that the gloomy impression of Baskerville Hall may have been caused partly by fatigue and the journey. He remains at the Hall after breakfast to examine papers while Dr. Watson investigates the neighborhood.

l: Stapleton, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 7.
s: Jack Stapleton introduces himself to Dr. Watson as a naturalist living at Merripit House. He discusses the moor, the Grimpen Mire, the Baskerville family legend, and Sir Charles Baskerville’s death, and he claims to know safe paths through the mire. He pursues a rare insect, then returns and watches Beryl and Watson closely.

l: Mrs. Stapleton, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 7.
s: Beryl Stapleton approaches Dr. Watson on the moor and urgently warns him to return to London and never set foot on the moor again. When Jack Stapleton returns, she conceals the warning by pretending that she and Watson had been discussing the orchids.

l: Sherlock Holmes, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 7.
s: Sherlock Holmes has sent Dr. Watson to investigate the neighbors and has arranged a test telegram intended to determine whether Barrymore was in London. Watson hopes Holmes will soon be free to take responsibility for the case, but Holmes cannot leave town because of other cases.

l: Barrymore, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 7.
s: Barrymore tells Sir Henry that the woman’s sob heard during the night could not have come from his wife, although Watson later sees that Mrs. Barrymore has clearly been crying. The postmaster confirms that the telegram was delivered to Mrs. Barrymore while Barrymore was supposedly in the loft, leaving no proof that Barrymore had not been in London.

l: Sir Charles Baskerville, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 7.
s: Jack Stapleton says that he was fond of Sir Charles Baskerville and knew from Dr. Mortimer that Sir Charles had a weak heart. Stapleton believes Sir Charles may have seen a dog in the yew alley and died of fright.

l: Baskerville Hall, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 7.
s: In the morning sunlight, Baskerville Hall seems much less gloomy to Dr. Watson and Sir Henry than it had the previous evening. The Hall remains associated with the unexplained sobbing heard during the night and with suspicions surrounding Barrymore.

l: Merripit House, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 7.
s: Merripit House is the home of Jack and Beryl Stapleton, situated near the moor. Jack invites Dr. Watson to visit it and meet his sister, and Beryl approaches Watson from its direction.

l: Dartmoor, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 7.
s: The moor is portrayed as vast, barren, mysterious, and filled with unusual natural and prehistoric features. Jack Stapleton says he has explored it extensively, while Beryl warns Dr. Watson to leave it.

l: Grimpen Mire, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 7.
s: The Grimpen Mire is a dangerous bog in which a moor pony disappears and dies, with another pony apparently being swallowed while Watson and Jack watch. Jack claims that he can reach isolated areas within it by following complex landmarks, but warns Watson that entering it would almost certainly be fatal.

l: London, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 7.
s: London is the place to which Beryl Stapleton urgently tells Dr. Watson to return. Barrymore’s possible presence in London is also part of Watson’s investigation into the events surrounding Sir Charles Baskerville’s death.

l: the Hound of the Baskervilles, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 7.
s: The Baskerville hound is described as a fiend dog believed by local peasants to haunt the family and the moor. Jack Stapleton says many peasants claim to have seen it, though he suggests that Sir Charles’s fear of such a creature may have contributed to his death.

l: Sir Charles Baskerville's death, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 7.
s: Dr. Watson continues to question the circumstances of Sir Charles Baskerville’s death, including Barrymore’s movements and the possibility that someone pursued Sir Charles. Jack Stapleton suggests that Sir Charles died of fright after seeing a dog because of his weak heart.

l: the legend of the Hound of the Baskervilles, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 7.
s: The Baskerville family legend concerns a fiend dog said to haunt the family. Jack Stapleton calls the peasants credulous but admits that the legend strongly affected Sir Charles.

l: the Hound's cry, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 7.
s: A long, mournful cry rises over the moor while Dr. Watson and Jack Stapleton are walking. The peasants identify it as the Hound of the Baskervilles calling for its prey, while Jack proposes that it may have been caused by bogs or the cry of a rare bittern.

l: The Hound of the Baskervilles, The Hound of the Baskervilles, A short walk brought us to it, a bleak moorland house, once the
s: Dr. Watson visits Stapleton and Beryl Stapleton at their bleak moorland house, where Stapleton explains their former life and present interests. Beryl initially warns Watson to take Sir Henry away from the moor, then follows him to withdraw the warning and attributes it to fears about the Baskerville curse. Watson remains troubled by the death of Sir Charles, the mysterious sound linked to the hound, and the danger surrounding Sir Henry. Beryl says she cannot provide any definite information and returns before her brother notices her absence.

l: Dr. Watson, The Hound of the Baskervilles, A short walk brought us to it, a bleak moorland house, once the
s: Dr. Watson visits Stapleton and Beryl Stapleton at their moorland house and discusses their life there. He questions Beryl about her warning to Sir Henry and promises to convey it, but leaves without learning anything definite.

l: Stapleton, The Hound of the Baskervilles, A short walk brought us to it, a bleak moorland house, once the
s: Stapleton lives with Beryl in a repaired former farm on the moor. He says that he formerly ran a school, which was devastated by an epidemic, and that he now devotes himself to botany and zoology. He plans to visit Sir Henry and make his acquaintance.

l: Mrs. Stapleton, The Hound of the Baskervilles, A short walk brought us to it, a bleak moorland house, once the
s: Beryl Stapleton lives with her brother and says that she is devoted to Nature and is never dull. She first warns Dr. Watson to take Sir Henry away from the moor, then follows Watson to retract or qualify the warning, saying it arose from fears connected with the Baskerville curse. She says her brother would be angry if he knew she had tried to make Sir Henry leave.

l: Sir Henry Baskerville, The Hound of the Baskervilles, A short walk brought us to it, a bleak moorland house, once the
s: Sir Henry is the new member of the Baskerville family living at Baskerville Hall. Beryl is distressed that he has come to the moor and believes he will face danger there, while Stapleton intends to visit him.

l: bleak moorland house, The Hound of the Baskervilles, A short walk brought us to it, a bleak moorland house, once the
s: The bleak moorland house was once a prosperous grazier's farm but has been repaired and converted into a modern dwelling. Its stunted orchard and surrounding moor give it a mean and melancholy appearance, although the interior has large, elegant rooms.

l: Dartmoor, The Hound of the Baskervilles, A short walk brought us to it, a bleak moorland house, once the
s: The moor is described as bleak, granite-flecked, and stretching unbroken to the horizon. Watson associates it with melancholy, vague fears, and the danger believed to threaten the Baskerville family.

l: London, The Hound of the Baskervilles, A short walk brought us to it, a bleak moorland house, once the
s: Beryl urges Dr. Watson to have Sir Henry return to London rather than remain at the place she considers dangerous.

l: Baskerville Hall, The Hound of the Baskervilles, A short walk brought us to it, a bleak moorland house, once the
s: Baskerville Hall is the place where Sir Henry has come to live. Beryl says Stapleton wants the Hall inhabited because he believes this would benefit the poor people of the moor.

l: Grimpen Mire, The Hound of the Baskervilles, A short walk brought us to it, a bleak moorland house, once the
s: Dr. Watson compares his life on the moor to Grimpen Mire, with its deceptive green patches into which a person may sink and no guide to show the safe path.

l: Sir Charles Baskerville's death, The Hound of the Baskervilles, A short walk brought us to it, a bleak moorland house, once the
s: Beryl and Stapleton were deeply shocked by the death of Sir Charles, whom they knew intimately because he often walked across the moor to their house. Beryl says the tragedy strengthened her fear that the Baskerville family's curse had some basis.

l: warning to Sir Henry, The Hound of the Baskervilles, A short walk brought us to it, a bleak moorland house, once the
s: Beryl's warning tells Sir Henry to leave the moor and avoid the place that has supposedly been fatal to his family. She later tells Watson that she has done her duty but cannot give any definite information about the danger.

l: the legend of the Hound of the Baskervilles, The Hound of the Baskervilles, A short walk brought us to it, a bleak moorland house, once the
s: Beryl says that Sir Charles was deeply impressed by the curse hanging over the Baskerville family. After his death, she felt there were grounds for fearing that the curse was connected with danger to Sir Henry.

l: The Hound of the Baskervilles, The Hound of the Baskervilles, A short walk brought us to it, a bleak moorland house, once the
s: Beryl refers to the story of the hound and says that she believes in it, while Dr. Watson dismisses it as nonsense.

l: the danger on the moor, The Hound of the Baskervilles, A short walk brought us to it, a bleak moorland house, once the
s: Beryl believes Sir Henry will run a danger by living at a place that has always been fatal to his family. She cannot identify the danger or provide Dr. Watson with definite information about it.

l: The Hound of the Baskervilles, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 8.
s: Dr. John Watson writes a report to Mr. Sherlock Holmes from Baskerville Hall about Sir Henry Baskerville and the people and dangers surrounding him on the moor. He describes Sir Henry’s growing attraction to Miss Stapleton, Jack Stapleton’s apparent disapproval, and the continuing uncertainty surrounding the escaped convict. Watson also investigates Barrymore’s questionable behavior and observes him conducting a secret nighttime vigil at an upstairs window. Watson and Sir Henry have made a plan of campaign based on these observations, which Watson promises to explain in his next report.

l: Dr. Watson, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 8.
s: Dr. John Watson reports from Baskerville Hall to Mr. Sherlock Holmes, describing the moor, the household, local residents, and his suspicions about Barrymore. He observes Barrymore’s nighttime movements and discusses the matter with Sir Henry Baskerville.

l: Sherlock Holmes, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 8.
s: Mr. Sherlock Holmes receives Watson’s letters and telegrams about events at Baskerville Hall. He had instructed Watson never to allow Sir Henry Baskerville to go out alone and asked him to provide factual reports about the people around them.

l: Sir Henry Baskerville, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 8.
s: Sir Henry Baskerville becomes strongly attracted to Miss Stapleton and repeatedly refers to her after meeting her. He questions Jack Stapleton about supernatural interference in human affairs, confronts Barrymore about the test telegram, and works with Watson on a plan of campaign.

l: Stapleton, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 8.
s: Jack Stapleton shows guarded interest in the legend of the wicked Hugo and appears to share the popular view that an evil influence may affect families. He repeatedly prevents Sir Henry Baskerville and Miss Stapleton from being alone and appears strongly disapproving of their growing intimacy.

l: Mrs. Stapleton, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 8.
s: Miss Stapleton is described as beautiful, fascinating, tropical, and exotic, in contrast to her cool and unemotional brother. She appears to return Sir Henry Baskerville’s attraction, while Jack Stapleton seems intent on preventing their intimacy from developing.

l: Barrymore, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 8.
s: Barrymore confirms that he received the test telegram, though his wife brought it to him and wrote the reply after he instructed her what to say. Watson later sees him walking barefoot through Baskerville Hall at night, holding a candle to a window and staring expectantly across the moor before extinguishing the light.

l: Mrs. Barrymore, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 8.
s: Mrs. Barrymore is described as heavy, solid, intensely respectable, and puritanical. Despite her unemotional appearance, she has repeatedly been seen with traces of tears, suggesting a deep sorrow or troubling secret.

l: Selden, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 8.
s: The escaped convict has not been seen or heard from for a fortnight, leading the local people to believe that he has left the moor. Watson considers it unlikely that he could have survived there so long without food, although the stone huts would provide hiding places.

l: Baskerville Hall, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 8.
s: Baskerville Hall is the isolated household from which Watson sends his report and where he, Sir Henry Baskerville, and other residents live under concern about the escaped convict. Watson believes that secret business is occurring inside the house.

l: Dartmoor, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 8.
s: The moor is portrayed as vast, grim, isolated, and filled with prehistoric huts, graves, and monoliths. It provides hiding places for the escaped convict and forms the dark landscape watched by Barrymore during his nighttime vigil.

l: the letters to Holmes, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 8.
s: Watson’s letters to Mr. Sherlock Holmes record events and preserve his feelings and suspicions more accurately than memory. One page is missing, but the remaining letters are described as exactly written.

l: the reports to Holmes, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 8.
s: Watson’s previous letters and telegrams have kept Mr. Sherlock Holmes informed about events at Baskerville Hall. Watson says that he had little important to report until the surprising events described in this unit and promises that his next report will explain the plan of campaign.

l: the legend of the Hound of the Baskervilles, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 8.
s: The legend associated with the Baskerville family remains a subject of discussion at the place where the story of the wicked Hugo supposedly began. Jack Stapleton gives guarded answers about supernatural interference and leaves the impression that he shares the popular belief in an evil influence affecting families.

l: Sir Charles Baskerville's death, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 8.
s: Watson revisits the yew alley and the moor-gate to reconstruct the fatal night of the old gentleman’s death. He imagines that the man saw something terrifying on the moor, fled down the alley, and died from horror and exhaustion, while still wondering whether a human agency was involved.

l: Barrymore's secret nighttime vigil, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 8.
s: Barrymore’s secret nighttime vigil begins when he quietly leaves his room carrying a candle and enters an otherwise empty room. He holds the candle against the window, watches the darkness of the moor with rigid expectation, groans, extinguishes the light, and later returns; Watson also hears a key turn in a lock.

l: the Stapleton–Sir Henry courtship, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 8.
s: Sir Henry Baskerville and Miss Stapleton appear mutually attracted after their first meeting. Jack Stapleton repeatedly prevents them from being alone and shows disapproval, despite the apparent advantages of their possible marriage.

l: the plan of campaign, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 8.
s: Watson and Sir Henry Baskerville create a plan of campaign based on Watson’s observations of Barrymore’s nighttime behavior. Watson does not yet reveal its details, reserving them for a later report.

l: The Hound of the Baskervilles, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 9.
s: Dr. Watson reports that Barrymore appears to watch the moor from a particular western window at night, leading him and Sir Henry Baskerville to plan to observe Barrymore. Sir Henry goes onto the moor alone, but Watson follows and witnesses him meeting Miss Stapleton, whose brother Stapleton angrily interrupts their conversation. Sir Henry tells Watson that he proposed marriage to Miss Stapleton, but Stapleton opposed the relationship and demanded that the matter rest for three months. Stapleton later apologizes, and Sir Henry agrees to dine at Merripit House while limiting himself to Miss Stapleton’s friendship.

l: Dr. Watson, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 9.
s: Dr. Watson examines Barrymore’s movements, reports them to Sir Henry Baskerville, and follows Sir Henry onto the moor despite Sherlock Holmes’s instructions not to leave him alone. He witnesses the meeting between Sir Henry and Miss Stapleton, then tells Sir Henry what he saw and records the events for Holmes.

l: Sherlock Holmes, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 9.
s: Sherlock Holmes had instructed Dr. Watson not to leave Sir Henry Baskerville, especially not to let him go alone upon the moor. Watson tries to follow those instructions despite Sir Henry’s objections.

l: Sir Henry Baskerville, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 9.
s: Sir Henry agrees with Dr. Watson to watch Barrymore at night, but later insists on going alone onto the moor. He meets Miss Stapleton, proposes marriage to her, quarrels with Stapleton over the relationship, and agrees to let the matter rest for three months while cultivating her friendship.

l: Barrymore, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 9.
s: Barrymore is known to walk through the passages at night and is seen watching from the western window of Baskerville Hall. Sir Henry and Dr. Watson suspect that he is looking for someone or something on the moor.

l: Stapleton, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 9.
s: Stapleton sees Sir Henry with Miss Stapleton on the moor and runs toward them in great anger, interrupting their conversation and taking his sister away. He later apologizes to Sir Henry, explaining that he feared losing his sister, and the breach between them is healed.

l: Mrs. Stapleton, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 9.
s: Miss Stapleton meets Sir Henry on the moor and speaks earnestly about the danger of the place, urging him to leave. She appears reluctant when Sir Henry embraces her and accepts Stapleton’s intervention without protest.

l: Baskerville Hall, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 9.
s: Baskerville Hall is being prepared for major renovation and refurnishing. Sir Henry has engaged an architect, a London contractor, decorators, and furnishers to restore the grandeur of his family home.

l: Dartmoor, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 9.
s: The moor can be viewed most clearly from the western window of Baskerville Hall, and Barrymore appears to watch it at night. Sir Henry and Miss Stapleton meet there, where she warns that it is a place of danger.

l: Merripit House, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 9.
s: Merripit House is associated with Miss Stapleton and Stapleton. Sir Henry and Dr. Watson are to dine there the following Friday as a sign that the quarrel between Sir Henry and Stapleton has ended.

l: Barrymore's secret nighttime vigil, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 9.
s: Barrymore’s nocturnal watch takes place from a western window of Baskerville Hall that overlooks the nearest part of the moor through an opening between two trees. Sir Henry and Dr. Watson plan to sit up and follow him to discover what he is watching.

l: Sir Henry and Miss Stapleton's meeting, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 9.
s: Sir Henry and Miss Stapleton meet by appointment on the moor and engage in a serious conversation. Miss Stapleton warns him about the danger, while Stapleton observes them, interrupts angrily, and leads her away.

l: Sir Henry's proposal to Miss Stapleton, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 9.
s: Sir Henry tells Miss Stapleton that he loves her and proposes that she marry him. Before she can answer, Stapleton arrives and objects angrily to Sir Henry’s attentions.

l: Stapleton's confrontation with Sir Henry, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 9.
s: Stapleton confronts Sir Henry after seeing him with Miss Stapleton and demands to know why he is paying her attentions. The confrontation becomes angry, but Stapleton later apologizes and withdraws his opposition temporarily.

l: the danger on the moor, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 9.
s: Miss Stapleton repeatedly warns Sir Henry that the moor is a place of danger and says she will not be happy until he has left it. Sir Henry does not wish to leave after meeting her, offering instead to take her with him through marriage.

l: romantic love and marriage, The Hound of the Baskervilles, Chapter 9.
s: Sir Henry is strongly infatuated with Miss Stapleton and believes that she returns his feelings. He proposes marriage, but Stapleton’s opposition and Miss Stapleton’s warnings prevent an immediate answer, and Sir Henry agrees to postpone the matter for three months.

l: The Hound of the Baskervilles, The Hound of the Baskervilles, So there is one of our small mysteries cleared up. It is
s: Dr. Watson and Sir Henry Baskerville discover that John and Eliza Barrymore have been secretly signaling to and feeding Eliza’s escaped brother, Selden, on the moor. They pursue Selden but fail to capture him after he throws a rock and runs away. During the pursuit, they hear the cry on the moor, which Sir Henry believes is the cry of the Hound of the Baskervilles. Watson also sees a mysterious tall man standing on a tor, but the figure disappears before he and Sir Henry can investigate.

l: Dr. Watson, The Hound of the Baskervilles, So there is one of our small mysteries cleared up. It is
s: Dr. Watson works with Sir Henry Baskerville to uncover the Barrymores’ nighttime activities and reports the explanation to Sherlock Holmes. He helps pursue Selden across the moor, hears the strange cry, and sees a tall, unidentified man silhouetted on a tor.

l: Sherlock Holmes, The Hound of the Baskervilles, So there is one of our small mysteries cleared up. It is
s: Sherlock Holmes is the intended recipient of Dr. Watson’s report and had sent Watson to investigate the case. Watson asks him to judge the progress of the investigation.

l: Sir Henry Baskerville, The Hound of the Baskervilles, So there is one of our small mysteries cleared up. It is
s: Sir Henry Baskerville helps Watson confront the Barrymores and learns that they have been assisting Selden. He joins Watson in trying to capture Selden, becomes frightened by the cry on the moor, and believes it may have been the Hound of the Baskervilles.

l: Barrymore, The Hound of the Baskervilles, So there is one of our small mysteries cleared up. It is
s: John Barrymore is discovered holding a candle at a second-floor window as a signal. He admits that he has been helping his wife feed Selden, and Sir Henry allows him and Eliza to remain in service after hearing the explanation.

l: Mrs. Barrymore, The Hound of the Baskervilles, So there is one of our small mysteries cleared up. It is
s: Eliza Barrymore reveals that Selden is her younger brother and that the nighttime signal is used to communicate with him. She accepts responsibility for asking John Barrymore to help feed and protect Selden on the moor.

l: Selden, The Hound of the Baskervilles, So there is one of our small mysteries cleared up. It is
s: Selden is identified as Eliza Barrymore’s younger brother and an escaped convict hiding on the moor. Watson and Sir Henry find him by his signal light, but he escapes after throwing a rock and outrunning them.

l: Baskerville Hall, The Hound of the Baskervilles, So there is one of our small mysteries cleared up. It is
s: Baskerville Hall is the place from which the Barrymores send a candle signal to Selden. The signal tells him that food is ready and helps him identify where to collect it.

l: Dartmoor, The Hound of the Baskervilles, So there is one of our small mysteries cleared up. It is
s: The moor is where Selden hides while the Barrymores secretly provide him with food. Watson and Sir Henry cross it during their pursuit, hear a frightening cry there, and observe a mysterious tall man on a tor.
